## Where we are

::: {.incremental}
- Session 1: ordered vs nominal outcomes; cumulative proportions
- Today: the **proportional-odds model** for an ordered outcome
- By the end you can:
  - fit it with `MASS::polr` and read **odds ratios**
  - explain the **thresholds**
  - give **predicted probabilities** for each category
:::

# Topic 1 — The model {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## Cumulative logits

::: {.eq}
logit P(Y ≤ k) = ζ~k~ − (β~1~x~1~ + β~2~x~2~ + …)     k = 1, 2, 3
:::

::: {.incremental}
- One **threshold** ζ~k~ for each cut-point between categories (3 for 4 categories)
- **One set of coefficients** β shared by all cut-points: the **proportional-odds** (parallel lines) assumption
- exp(β) is the **odds ratio for being in a higher category**: the same whichever cut-point you look at
- In `polr`, β > 0 means **higher categories** (worse anaemia) are more likely
:::

## One predictor

```{r}
m1 <- MASS::polr(anaemia ~ wealth, data = mat, Hess = TRUE)
round(exp(cbind(OR = coef(m1), confint(m1))), 2)
m1$zeta |> round(2)
```

::: {.key}
**OR = `r round(exp(coef(m1)), 2)` per wealth quintile**: each quintile higher multiplies the **odds of being in a worse anaemia category** by about `r round(exp(coef(m1)), 2)` (a **`r round(100 * (1 - exp(coef(m1))))`% reduction**), **at every cut-point** (None vs worse, up to Moderate vs Severe).
:::

# Topic 2 — An adjusted model {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## Several predictors

```{r}
m2 <- MASS::polr(anaemia ~ wealth + education + bmi + anc_visits + parity + age + tribal + residence, data = mat, Hess = TRUE)
round(exp(cbind(OR = coef(m2), confint(m2))), 2)     # tbl_regression(m2, exponentiate = TRUE) formats this for a paper
```

## Reading the adjusted odds ratios

::: {.incremental}
- **Wealth, higher education, BMI and antenatal visits** are protective (OR below 1)
- **Parity** goes slightly the other way
- The OR for **tribal group** is only about `r round(exp(coef(m2))[["tribalYes"]], 1)`: **do not trust it yet**. Session 3 shows the model is wrong for that variable
- `confint()` gives profile-likelihood CIs; p-values come from the t value (|t| above about 2)
:::

## Thresholds

::: {.eq}
None|Mild: ζ~1~    Mild|Moderate: ζ~2~    Moderate|Severe: ζ~3~
:::

They are the **baseline log-odds** of each cumulative probability (when all predictors are 0) and are **not** of substantive interest. **K categories need K − 1 thresholds.**

# Topic 3 — Predicted probabilities {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## What it means for a woman

```{r}
nd <- data.frame(wealth = c(1, 5), education = factor("Primary", levels = levels(mat$education)), bmi = 20.5, anc_visits = 3, parity = 2, age = 27,
                 tribal = factor("No", levels = c("No", "Yes")), residence = factor("Rural", levels = c("Urban", "Rural")))
rownames(nd) <- c("poorest", "richest")
round(predict(m2, newdata = nd, type = "probs"), 2)
```

::: {.incremental}
- Probability of **each** category for a given profile: the four numbers add to 1
- The **poorest** woman has about a **10% chance of severe anaemia**; the **richest** about **3%**
- Clearer for readers than odds ratios: report **both**
:::

## Compared with a binary model

```{r}
c(ordinal = unname(exp(coef(m1))), binary_any_vs_none = unname(exp(coef(glm(I(anaemia != "None") ~ wealth, family = binomial, data = mat)))["wealth"])) |> round(2)
```

When proportional odds holds, the ordinal and the binary ORs agree, but the **ordinal model uses the severity too**, so it is **more precise**.

## Reporting an ordinal model

::: {.good}
- State the **outcome order** and the **model** (cumulative-logit, proportional odds)
- **Odds ratios** with CIs, and say they are for **a higher category**
- A few **predicted probabilities**
- The **assumption check** (next session)
:::

## Self-check quiz (1/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("s2q1", "A proportional-odds model gives OR = 0.57 per wealth quintile. Which is the best reading?",
         c("Each quintile higher lowers the anaemia grade by 0.57 categories on average",
           "Women in the top quintile have 57% of the anaemia of the poorest women",
           "Each quintile higher multiplies the odds of a worse category by 0.57",
           "The probability of anaemia is 0.57 for each one of the quintiles"), answer = 3,
         explain = "The OR compares odds of being in a higher category versus lower ones, and under proportional odds it is the same at every cut-point.")
```

## Self-check quiz (2/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("s2q2", "Why does a model for a four-category outcome have three thresholds?",
         c("Three of the four categories are used up as references",
           "There are three cut-points between four ordered categories",
           "The model needs one separate threshold for each predictor",
           "Four categories need four thresholds minus one for the intercept"), answer = 2,
         explain = "A K-category outcome has K - 1 cumulative probabilities, so K - 1 thresholds (intercepts).")
```

## Self-check quiz (3/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("s2q3", "What is the proportional-odds assumption?",
         c("The categories of the outcome are equally spaced in terms of severity",
           "The predictors are proportional to the outcome on the log-odds scale",
           "Each predictor's effect is the same at every cut-point of the outcome",
           "The odds of each single category are equal in all of the groups"), answer = 3,
         explain = "One set of coefficients applies to all cumulative logits, so each odds ratio is constant across cut-points. Equal spacing is not assumed.")
```

## Self-check quiz (4/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("s2q4", "Why are predicted probabilities useful alongside odds ratios?",
         c("They are always more accurate than the odds ratios from the same model",
           "They remove the need to check the model assumptions of the analysis",
           "They show whether each of the thresholds is significant or not",
           "They give the chance of each category on a scale readers understand"), answer = 4,
         explain = "Odds ratios are on a log-odds scale that is hard to grasp; predicted probabilities show what the model implies for a woman with a given profile.")
```

## Self-check quiz (5/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("s2q5", "In polr, a positive coefficient for a predictor means what?",
         c("Higher values make the higher (worse) categories more likely",
           "Higher values make the lower categories more likely to be seen",
           "The predictor is significant at the 5% level in the sample",
           "The predictor reduces all of the thresholds to exactly zero"), answer = 1,
         explain = "In the usual polr parametrisation, positive coefficients move the probability up the ordered scale, towards the last category.")
```

## Score and take-home

**Your score: <span class="quiz-score"></span>**

::: {.incremental}
- **Proportional-odds**: one OR per predictor, the same at every cut-point
- exp(β) = odds of a **higher category**; K categories → **K − 1 thresholds**
- Report **ORs with CI** and **predicted probabilities**
- The single OR is only trustworthy if the **assumption holds**
:::
